# Joint profiles and residual roots exclude an exact planar volume triple

This note proves a scoped arbitrary-shape theorem, not general three-fiber
OC. The new ingredient is the interaction of actual critical-cap cover
profiles with a uniform residual-root upper bound on their middle masses.

## 1. Setting and elementary critical-cap facts

Let d>=2. Let A,K,B be positive d-dimensional compact convex bodies at
integer coordinates -1,0,1, with (A+B)/2 contained in K. Normalize their
volumes to a,1,b with 0<a<=b; this is a common scaling of continuous
coordinates only. Put Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d and M=1+a+b.

Suppose y in K is a middle-fiber depth maximizer, with raw depth Q. A
critical cap is an actual closed ambient halfspace

    H_i={u_i.(x-y)+beta_i z>=0}, u_i nonzero,

whose three captured volumes U_i,q_i,V_i sum to Q. By varying beta_i
until A is fully captured and B empty, and then in the opposite direction,
we obtain

    U_i+V_i<=min(a,b)=a.                                 (1)

All comparisons use finite tilts: the fibers are compact. Boundary
hyperplanes of a nonzero continuous normal have zero d-volume.

The finite-tilt/active-normal theorem, fully proved in
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`, gives
continuity of middle depth, attainment by finite tilts, and, at an interior
maximum, a family of at most d+1 actual critical caps with

    sum lambda_i u_i=0, lambda_i>0.                       (2)

The maximum is interior. At a boundary point of K use a supporting
continuous direction whose own cap volume is zero. As the integer tilt
varies, the endpoint captured volumes vary continuously in opposite
monotone directions and agree at some finite tilt. A positive common
volume would give a positive-volume Minkowski midpoint in the zero-volume
middle cap, by ordinary BM. The common volume therefore is zero, and
boundary depth is zero. In contrast the ordinary centroid of K has mixed
depth at least Gamma>0, from the contribution of its own fiber. Thus a
middle maximum lies in int K, and (2) applies.

The middle traces in (2) cover all R^d. Put Delta=sum lambda_i beta_i.
Their traces at integer z have weighted signed margin z Delta. Therefore
at least one endpoint is also covered: B if Delta>=0 and A if Delta<=0.
Let E be such an endpoint and e its volume; always e>=a. These are the
same actual ambient caps, with their actual individual integer tilts.

## 2. A uniform upper bound from residual BM

Assume the nonheavy inequalities

    a<=M/2, 1<=M/2, b<=M/2,

and 0<Q<=T:=Gamma M/2. Whole-body BM gives

    a^(1/d)+b^(1/d)<=2.                                  (3)

In particular a<=1. Also b<=1+a, so T<=Gamma(1+a)<=2Gamma<1.
Define F_Q on [max(0,Q-a),1] by

    F_Q(q)=(a-Q+q)^(1/d)+b^(1/d)-2(1-q)^(1/d).

It is continuous and strictly increasing, is positive at 1, and is
negative at its left endpoint. For Q<a the last assertion follows from
(a-Q)^(1/d)<a^(1/d) and (3). For Q>=a, put q0=Q-a. Since

    1-q0=1+a-Q >= (1-Gamma)(1+a) >= (1-Gamma)b > b/2,

one has F_Q(q0)<b^(1/d)-2(b/2)^(1/d)<0. Consequently there is a unique
root h(Q) in (max(0,Q-a),1). This root is strictly increasing in Q:
increasing Q decreases F_Q wherever both expressions are defined, and
if its new left endpoint passes the old root, the new root is larger
for that reason directly.

Every actual critical middle mass obeys

    q_i<=min(Q,h(Q)).                                    (4)

Indeed let c=U_i+V_i=Q-q_i<=a by (1). If c=a, then q_i=Q-a<h(Q).
Otherwise c<a, so both endpoint residual volumes a-U_i and b-V_i are
strictly positive. Their residual sets lie on the strict excluded side
of the same ambient cut. Midpoint inclusion followed by ordinary BM
therefore gives

    (a-U_i)^(1/d)+(b-V_i)^(1/d)<=2(1-q_i)^(1/d).          (5)

One can apply BM first to compact strict subcuts and pass upwards; no
supporting-plane boundary mass occurs, as all fibers have positive
d-dimensional volume and u_i is nonzero.

For fixed c, the left side of (5), considered as a function of
U_i in [0,c] with V_i=c-U_i, is concave, and hence is minimized at an
endpoint. The smaller endpoint value is obtained at U_i=c,V_i=0:
the decrement t^(1/d)-(t-c)^(1/d) decreases with t, and a<=b. Hence

    (a-Q+q_i)^(1/d)+b^(1/d)<=2(1-q_i)^(1/d).             (6)

Thus F_Q(q_i)<=0 and (4) follows. Empty and supporting captured sets are
allowed; the argument only requires positive residuals in the c<a case.
The exceptional full-small-endpoint case was handled separately.

## 3. Safe cap-count profiles in every dimension d>=2

For any finite halfspace cover of a positive convex body D, with cap
volumes t_i, the ordinary distal profile is

    sum_i(t_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/Gamma >= |D|, alpha>=0.   (7)

For completeness, trim from each cap its distal parallel subcap of
volume (t_i-alpha)_+. If their union already has volume at least |D|,
(7) is immediate. Otherwise the retained compact convex body has volume
at least |D|-sum(t_i-alpha)_+, while every original cap retains at most
alpha. Its ordinary centroid lies in at least one original cap, because
the family covers D. Ordinary Grünbaum bounds the retained volume by
alpha/Gamma and proves (7). Boundary hyperplanes are null. Distal cuts
of the prescribed volumes exist by continuity of one-dimensional tails.

Set kappa=1/Gamma-2, so 0<kappa<1. For m>=3, substitute into (7) the
third-largest t_i. The resulting necessary condition is

    t_largest+t_second+kappa t_third >= |D|.             (8)

For any m this weighted sum of the three largest entries is
coordinatewise increasing. This monotonicity is why (8) is used instead
of a minimum-entry formula whose coefficient can be negative for m>=4.

Order the middle cap masses q_1<=...<=q_m. If m>=3, (8) for K gives

    q_m+q_(m-1)+kappa q_(m-2)>=1.                        (9)

The covered endpoint's masses W_i satisfy W_i<=Q-q_i. Applying (8),
then its coordinatewise monotonicity, gives

    q_1+q_2+kappa q_3 <= Q/Gamma-e <= Q/Gamma-a.         (10)

Equations (4), (9), and (10) are safe all-dimensional necessary
conditions. They make no claim that arbitrarily assigned volume arrays
with these properties come from convex bodies or actual critical caps.

For exactly three caps, multiply (10) by kappa and combine it with (9).
The q_1 terms cancel, yielding

    1+kappa a <= kappa Q/Gamma
                       +(1-kappa)q_2+(1-kappa^2)q_3
                 <= kappa Q/Gamma
                       +(1-kappa)(2+kappa)h(Q).         (11)

The first inequality can also retain e>=a. For two or fewer caps,
ordinary union bounds for K and E give mQ>=1+e. These statements do
not assert that a circuit has at most three caps in dimensions above two.

## 4. Exact theorem for arbitrary planar shapes

**Theorem.** Let A,K,B be planar convex bodies with

    (A+B)/2 subset K,   (|A|,|K|,|B|)=(1/4,1,121/100).

For S=({-1} times A) union ({0} times K) union ({1} times B), there
exists (0,y) in S whose raw depth is strictly greater than

    Gamma_2 H_2(S)/2=41/75,  Gamma_2=4/9.

Thus the exact OC lower bound holds for every compatible shape triple
with these volume ratios. The conclusion includes all closed ambient
halfspaces in R^3.

**Proof.** Write a=1/4,b=121/100,T=41/75. The total mass is 123/50,
and all three fibers are strictly nonheavy. Suppose the actual middle
maximum Q satisfies Q<=T. Its positive projected critical circuit has
at most three caps by Section 1. One cap cannot have a positive dependence
of nonzero continuous normals. For two caps, mQ>=1+e>=5/4 implies
Q>=5/8>T, a contradiction. Hence there are exactly three caps.

We prove the strict uniform bound

    q_i<x:=302/675.                                     (12)

If q_i<=Q-a, then q_i<=T-a=89/300<x. Otherwise the endpoint captured
sum Q-q_i is less than a, and (6) applies. If q_i>=x, its left-minus-right
side is at least

    sqrt(s)+sqrt(b)-2sqrt(t),
    s=a-T+x=407/2700,   t=1-x=373/675.                  (13)

This expression is strictly positive, with an exact rational certificate:

    4t-b=2701/2700>0,
    Z:=4t+b-s=2207/675>0,
    16bt-Z^2=703/91125>0.                              (14)

Indeed 4sqrt(bt)>Z. Consequently s>(2sqrt(t)-sqrt(b))^2; the latter
inner expression is positive by 4t>b. Taking its positive square root
proves (13)>0. This contradicts (6), and proves (12).

Here kappa=1/4. The first inequality in (11), retaining the actual
q_2,q_3 and using (12), gives

    1+a/4 < (9/16)T+(27/16)x=17/16=1+a/4.

The equality is exact rational arithmetic. This contradiction proves
Q>T. The chosen middle maximizer is one deterministic point of S;
its depth is defined over every ambient closed halfspace. This proves
the theorem. □

## 5. Scope and measure checks

The theorem is homogeneous under a common positive scaling of all fiber
areas, so it applies to area ratios (1/4,1,121/100), not just the displayed
normalization. Such scaling acts only on continuous coordinates and
preserves the mixed lattice and full halfspace family. If these are the
only three integer fibers of an ambient convex body, their midpoint
inclusion is automatic. Conversely the statement was proved directly
for every compatible triple, without additional regularity assumptions.

All three fibers have positive planar volume. Their embedded H_2
measures equal their areas, their finite union has H_2 measure 123/50,
and its Hausdorff dimension is two. Pure integer halfspaces are included
in the raw depth via the finite-tilt compactification theorem; they are
not discarded by considering the active nonzero continuous normals.
No rational approximation, varying-fiber limit, centroid rounding,
or ordinary whole-body BM equality is used.

The general conditions (4), (9), (10) leave other volume triples and
larger cap circuits unclosed. This result supersedes only the example
of an unexcluded actual volume triple in Section 5 of
`candidate 3c03d862047ffba9`.
That note's individual formal cap row remains arithmetically valid,
but cannot extend to an actual below-target critical covering menu for
these volume ratios, as just proved.

## 6. Provenance of the scalar bound and effective cap count

The root-depletion principle used in Section 2 is already proved in the
more general weighted setting in
`candidate 02239b6c4bf9e8a6`. Here its
two-endpoint specialization uses the actual remaining cap budget Q-q,
the genuine finite-tilt constraint Q-q<=a, and the separate c=a case.
The new exclusion comes from coupling that bound to both covered-body
profiles of one actual critical circuit, not from claiming a new general
Brunn--Minkowski principle.

The stronger ordinary effective-cap-count theorem in
`candidate 55fd8fec61360536` supplies (7) with
Gamma replaced by gamma_s, s=min(d,m-1), for a cover by m halfspaces.
Thus for a three-cap circuit in any d>=2, the two profiles may use
Gamma_2=4/9 even though the residual roots retain exponent 1/d and the
OC target retains Gamma_d. In that case (11) improves to

    4+a <= (9/4)Q+(27/4)h(Q).

This is a conditional three-cap necessary inequality in higher dimension;
Caratheodory does not guarantee three caps there. For more caps the
same effective theorem improves the profile coefficient, but the
top-three coordinate ordering and actual circuit size must still be
tracked. None of these remarks changes the planar certificate.
